###### Abstract.

A fundamental intent asymmetry plagues modern 3D asset creation: while
state-of-the-art 3D toolchains demand precise, executable parameters,
ordinary users typically provide vague, underspecified instructions.
Current 3D agents treat this ambiguity as noise, defaulting to blind
execution under a single-turn assumption. To address this limitation, we
introduce Clare, a clarification-aware and evolutionary 3D agent that
treats intent asymmetry not as an execution error, but as an opportunity
for strategic dialogue. By decoupling the generation pipeline into four
specialized cognitive roles, Clare intercepts and resolves
underspecified instructions before invoking computationally expensive 3D
tools to seamlessly execute tasks across five diverse domains:
text-to-3D generation, single-view reconstruction, multi-view
reconstruction, point cloud editing, and post-processing. Crucially,
rather than relying on rigid manual rules, Clare self-evolves its
clarification policy via simulated multi-turn interactions. By
optimizing a Multi-turn Reward, the agent internalizes the delicate
balance between interaction efficiency and task completion. To
rigorously test this, we construct 3D-Clarify, a comprehensive benchmark
comprising 620 interaction scenarios with systematically injected
ambiguity, missing information, and mistaken details. Clare achieves
state-of-the-art performance, with 60.40% and 43.34% success rates on
single-step and multi-step tasks, respectively, more than doubling
existing baselines. Both quantitative and qualitative results
demonstrate that proactive clarification is the missing key to robust 3D
execution. Code is available at
[https://github.com/xyzhu1225/CLARE](https://github.com/xyzhu1225/CLARE).

###### Keywords: 

Proactive Clarification, 3D Tool Orchestration, Self-Evolving Agents

## 1. Introduction

The democratization of 3D content creation has become increasingly
critical across gaming, virtual reality, architectural visualization,
and industrial design. Recent advances in 3D foundation models have
enabled non-expert users to generate, reconstruct, and edit 3D assets
through natural language interfaces ([Lee et al., 2024](#bib.bib3);
[Jiang, 2024](#bib.bib4); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5)). However, a
fundamental intent asymmetry persists between what users naturally
express and what 3D systems strictly require. While state-of-the-art 3D
pipelines demand precise, executable parameters—such as explicit input
file paths, strict output formats, appropriate model choices, and
numerical quality constraints—ordinary users typically provide vague,
underspecified instructions. A user might request "reconstruct this
object" without providing the image, ask to "edit the chair" from a
point cloud without specifying which points to keep, or inadvertently
request incompatible parameters that lead to runtime failures.

Current 3D agent systems operate under a single-turn, well-specified
assumption: they expect complete and executable instructions in one
shot. When faced with underspecified requirements, these systems exhibit
three failure modes: (1) blind execution of ambiguous requests,
producing irrelevant outputs that waste computational resources; (2)
undetected parameter contradictions, causing cryptic runtime errors that
frustrate users; and (3) passive behavior, lacking mechanisms to
proactively identify and resolve information gaps. While general-purpose
agentic frameworks like ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)) and
Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)) enable iterative reasoning
in symbolic domains, they lack domain-specific mechanisms for detecting
3D-specific uncertainties—such as missing file paths, modality
mismatches, or model capability violations.

Our key insight is that effective 3D task execution requires a
progressive alignment paradigm: clarify before executing. Rather than
treating ambiguity as noise to be ignored, we posit that an intelligent
3D agent should (1) detect incomplete or mistaken requirements before
invocation, (2) engage in targeted multi-turn clarification to resolve
uncertainties, and (3) leverage domain knowledge to map user preferences
(e.g., "high quality", "fast") to appropriate 3D models and parameters.
Crucially, the decision of when to clarify versus when to execute is
itself learnable—excessive clarification increases interaction cost,
while premature execution risks failure.

To realize this vision, we introduce Clare (Clarification-aware and
Evolutionary 3D agent), a multi-agent framework
(Figure [1](#acmlabel1 "Figure 1 ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration"))
that transforms underspecified user requirements into executable 3D
workflows through structured collaboration. Clare decouples the
generation pipeline into four specialized roles: (1) Proactive Approver,
which gates execution by detecting ambiguity, missing information, and
mistaken details; (2) Contextual Summarizer, which distills multi-turn
dialogue into structured task specifications; (3) 3D-Aware Programmer,
which synthesizes executable code by mapping user constraints to
appropriate 3D tools; and (4) Feedback Provider, which closes the
interaction loop with human-readable status reports and targeted
clarification questions. Beyond inference-time collaboration, Clare
employs a self-evolution mechanism: it learns optimal clarification
policies through simulated interactions with a user agent that embodies
realistic information asymmetry, optimizing a Multi-turn Reward (MR)
that balances task completion against interaction efficiency. This
simulation-based optimization enables the agent to internalize
long-horizon decision making without manual annotation.

To rigorously evaluate Clare, we construct 3D-Clarify, a comprehensive
benchmark spanning five canonical 3D domains. Each task is
systematically perturbed with three types of underspecified
requirements—ambiguity, missing information, and mistaken
details—creating a "lazy user" simulation that tests an agent’s
clarification capability.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose Clare, the first multi-agent framework that systematically
  addresses underspecified user requirements in 3D task execution
  through proactive clarification and tool orchestration across five
  diverse domains: text-to-3D generation, single-view reconstruction,
  multi-view reconstruction, point cloud editing, and post-processing.
- •
  We introduce 3D-Clarify, a benchmark with 620 tasks and three types of
  controlled underspecification. By standardizing the evaluation of
  intent asymmetry, it provides a foundational testbed to drive future
  research towards more robust, interactive 3D generation systems.
- •
  We develop a self-evolution training paradigm that optimizes
  clarification policies via simulated user interactions and Multi-turn
  Reward (MR) optimization, enabling the agent to learn effective
  multi-turn decision making without manual annotation. This empowers
  the agent to dramatically elevate its execution success rate to 60.40%
  on single-step tasks and 43.34% on complex multi-step tasks, achieving
  robust performance with negligible interaction overhead.

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1. LLM-based Agents for 3D Tasks

Recent advances in large language models have enabled language-driven
control over complex software systems, including 3D generation and
reconstruction pipelines. In parallel, numerous agent reasoning
frameworks have been employed to enable LLMs to interact with the
external environment. For example, ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib6))
interleaves reasoning traces with task-specific actions, allowing the
agent to dynamically interact with the environment. Reflexion ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib7)) further introduces a feedback-driven learning
mechanism, enabling agents to improve subsequent decisions by reflecting
on execution outcomes and past failures.

Existing LLM-based 3D agents ([Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib12); [Chen et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib17); [Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib18); [Ai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)) are mostly designed around specific 3D workflows
rather than diverse task settings. By comparison, Clare targets a
substantially broader task space, seamlessly integrating text-to-3D,
reconstruction, point cloud editing, and post-processing. This
capability to handle multi-step compositions makes our framework not
only clarification-aware but also highly generalizable across unified 3D
executions.

### 2.2. Interactive Clarification

Interactive clarification has been widely studied in human-centered AI
systems ([Acikgoz et al., 2025a](#bib.bib15); [Acikgoz et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib14); [Qian et al., 2025a](#bib.bib10); [Qian et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib11); [Sun et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), where systems must
actively gather missing information through multi-turn interactions
before executing a task.

Existing work on interactive clarification can be broadly categorized
into three directions. First, methods focusing on information
elicitation ask follow-up questions to resolve underspecified
constraints ([Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib22)). Second, user-centric
frameworks explore interaction policy learning to balance task
completion against dialogue cost ([Chen et al., 2024b](#bib.bib23);
[Qian et al., 2025b](#bib.bib11); [Kudrinskii et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24)). Third, collaborative paradigms shift from passive
responses to active goal-oriented cooperation ([Zhang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib25); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)). Collectively,
these efforts establish clarification as a core decision-making
capability.

Our work differs by situating clarification specifically within the
fragile pipeline of 3D task execution. We treat dialogue not as an
auxiliary behavior, but as a prerequisite to prevent invalid tool
selections, parameter contradictions, and fatal downstream errors.

### 2.3. Self-Evolving Agents

Recent surveys ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)) suggest that the development of self-evolving agents
reflects a paradigm shift from static systems to adaptive, lifelong
agents that continuously improve through interaction.

However, self-evolving frameworks ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib20);
[Yuan et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)) primarily focus on general
language-centric reasoning, leaving domain-specific workflows like 3D
asset creation underexplored. Our work fills this gap by introducing a
3D-domain-aware self-evolution paradigm. By coupling the agent with a
stateful simulated user, we optimize clarification policies through
multi-turn trajectories. This allows the system to internalize the
delicate balance between interaction efficiency and reliable execution
under underspecified requirements.

## 3. Problem Formulation

We formulate the 3D task execution problem as a goal-oriented
interaction between a user and a 3D agent. Unlike traditional
single-turn generation, the user possesses a latent goal
$`\mathcal{G}^{*}=\{p_{in},f,c,\theta\}`$, which encompasses all
essential information: the input source $`p_{in}`$ (path or prompt), the
desired output format $`f`$, user preference constraints $`c`$ (e.g.,
quality, speed or other constraints), and task-specific parameters
$`\theta`$. The initial user query $`q_{0}`$ is often an incomplete or
noisy projection of $`\mathcal{G}^{*}`$. We formalize three types of
underspecified requirements:

- •
  Ambiguity: $`q_{0}`$ maps to a set of multiple candidate goals:
  $`q_{0}\implies\{\mathcal{G}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{G}_{n}\}`$.
- •
  Missing Info: $`q_{0}\subset\mathcal{G}^{*}`$, where one or more
  critical elements from $`\{p_{in},f,c,\theta\}`$ are absent from
  $`q_{0}`$.
- •
  Mistaken Details: $`q_{0}`$ contains explicit errors $`e`$ such that
  $`e`$ contradicts the physical constraints of the 3D environment or
  the logical consistency of $`\mathcal{G}^{*}`$. (e.g., offering wrong
  input files, out-of-bound parameters)

The interaction unfolds as a sequence of turns
$`T=\{(q_{0},m_{0}),\dots,\allowbreak(q_{K},m_{K})\}`$. At each turn
$`j`$, the agent generates a response based on the updated history
$`\mathcal{H}_{<j}`$:
$`\pi(q_{j},\mathcal{H}_{<j})\to(m_{j},\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec})`$,
where $`\mathcal{T}_{3D}`$ indicates appropriate 3D tools and
$`\theta_{exec}`$ corresponds to the execution parameters for solving
the task. $`(\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec})=\emptyset`$ if the agent
chooses to clarify rather than execute. This loop continues until the
user issues a “Quit” command or the interaction reaches the maximum turn
limit $`T_{max}`$.

Our objective is to learn an optimal policy $`\pi^{*}`$ that maximizes
the expected completion rate of the 3D execution result while minimizing
interaction cost:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

````math
\pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{V}(\text{Exec}(\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec}),\mathcal{G}^{*})-\lambda\cdot K\right]
``` |  |

where $`\text{Exec}(\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec})`$ denotes the output
of the 3D toolchain, $`\mathcal{V}(\cdot)\in[0,1]`$ is the value
function provided by an automated verifier that assesses the final task
completion rate, and $`\lambda`$ is a penalty for the total turns $`K`$.

## 4. The CLARE Framework: Coordination via Progressive Alignment

### 4.1. Architecture Overview

Handling 3D tasks involves inherent ambiguity: users often lack the
precise terminology to describe spatial geometry or rendering styles. We
introduce Clare, a multi-agent framework designed not merely to execute
commands, but to manage the uncertainty of human intent.
Figure [2](#acmlabel2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1. Architecture Overview ‣ 4. The CLARE Framework: Coordination via Progressive Alignment ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
shows a progressive alignment loop that decouples the complex generation
process into four specialized cognitive roles: Decision Gating, Context
Refinement, Executable Synthesis, and Feedback Alignment. This
separation of concerns ensures that ambiguous or mistaken requirements
are trapped and resolved before touching the computationally expensive
3D tools.

code.](2607.16352v1/method_pdf.png)

Figure 2. Architecture of Clare. Four specialized components collaborate

### 4.2. Core Components

##### Proactive Approver: The Cognitive Gatekeeper

Traditional agents often hallucinate parameters for vague instructions,
leading to wasted generation time. The Proactive Approver acts as the
first line of defense. It evaluates the completeness of the current
instruction $`q_{j}`$ against the conversation history. Instead of
blindly forwarding requests, it computes a binary decision state
$`d\in\{\textsc{Execute},\textsc{Clarify}\}`$. By detecting three
distinct types of requirements—Ambiguity, Missing Information, and
Mistaken Details—the Approver effectively "freezes" the execution
pipeline until the user’s intent is fully actionable, enforcing a
rigorous standard for task initiation.

##### Contextual Summarizer: Structured Intent Mining

Once approved, the Contextual Summarizer bridges the gap between
fragmented natural language and structured execution specifications. It
functions as the system’s dynamic memory, aggregating the multi-turn
dialogue history $`\mathcal{H}_{<j}`$ into a normalized task manifest
$`\mathcal{M}`$. This component performs crucial state tracking: it
resolves co-references (e.g., "remove it" referring to a previously
generated chair) and explicitly extracts constraints such as target file
paths and quality preferences. By distilling noise into a structured
schema, it provides a noise-free specification for the downstream
programmer.

##### 3D-Aware Programmer: Adaptive Tool Orchestration

Translating the Manifest $`\mathcal{M}`$ into code requires
domain-specific knowledge. The 3D-Aware Programmer goes beyond generic
code generation by incorporating a model selection knowledge base. It
understands the capability boundaries of different 3D tools. As detailed
in our implementation, the Programmer dynamically maps user-defined
constraints $`c`$ (e.g., "high quality", "fast speed") to specific model
$`\mathcal{T}_{3D}`$ and parameters $`\theta_{exec}`$. This ensures that
the synthesized Python code is not only syntactically correct but
physically and semantically grounded in the 3D generation context.

##### Interaction Feedback Provider: Closing the Semantic Gap

Effective collaboration requires two-way communication. The Feedback
Provider serves as the interface for conversational alignment. It
operates in two adaptive modes: Clarification Mode: When the Approver
rejects a request, this module translates the rejection reasoning into a
natural, targeted question, guiding the user to provide the missing bits
without cognitive overload. Status Reporting Mode: Post-execution, it
interprets raw execution logs and potential runtime errors, translating
them into human-readable summaries. This closes the loop, allowing users
to iteratively refine their 3D assets based on clear, actionable system
feedback.

### 4.3. Self-Evolution via Collaborative Simulation

Drawing inspiration from collaborative training frameworks ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)), we treat the 3D task execution as a long-term
optimization problem. Static datasets often fail to capture the nuances
of when to clarify versus when to execute. We address this by evolving
the agent’s policy $`\pi`$ through a Collaborative Simulation Loop,
maximizing a multi-turn reward derived from interactive trajectories
with a dynamic user simulator.

#### 4.3.1. Interactive Forward Sampling

To estimate the long-term utility of a clarification strategy, Clare
performs lookahead via simulation. Given a context
$`x=(q_{j},\mathcal{H}_{<j})`$, the agent samples $`N`$ candidate
responses $`\{m^{(1)},\dots,m^{(N)}\}`$ from its current policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$. For each candidate, we roll out a full interaction
trajectory $`\tau^{(i)}`$ by coupling the agent with a Simulated User
$`\mathcal{U}`$. This process reveals downstream consequences, helping
the agent separate vital clarifications from redundant, costly queries.

![Four side-by-side panels show the simulated-user specification
followed by benchmark examples for ambiguity, missing information, and

Figure 3. Overview of the 3D-Clarify benchmark. Each scenario starts

##### Simulated User with Hidden Goals

The Simulated User $`\mathcal{U}`$ is not a static responder but a
stateful agent designed to mimic realistic human behavior. Initialized
with a hidden target goal $`\mathcal{G}^{*}`$ (e.g., specific quality
and format constraints) and a surface-level vague query $`q_{0}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}`$ operates under an Information Asymmetry setting. As
detailed in our implementation, it follows strict behavioral stages:
initially providing vague requirements and only revealing critical
parameters when the agent explicitly identifies the information gap.
This "interaction friction" forces the agent to learn precise
interrogation strategies to unlock the hidden goal.

#### 4.3.2. Multi-turn Reward Formulation

We evaluate the quality of each sampled trajectory $`\tau`$ using a
composite Multi-turn Reward (MR), balancing task fidelity against
interaction efficiency. The reward is computed by an automated Verifier:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (2) |  |
``` math
MR(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(\text{Exec}(\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec}),\mathcal{G}^{*})-\lambda\cdot K
``` |  |

where $`K`$ is the number of interaction turns, and $`\lambda`$ acts as
a penalty coefficient to discourage verbosity. The verification function
$`\mathcal{V}\in[0,1]`$ assesses the semantic and parametric accuracy of
the final 3D output:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
\mathcal{V}=\mathbb{I}(\text{Type}_{\text{pred}}=\text{Type}_{\text{gt}})\cdot\left[\frac{1}{|\Theta|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\Theta|}\phi(\theta_{i},\theta_{i}^{*})\right]
``` |  |

Here, $`\mathbb{I}(\cdot)`$ ensures the fundamental task type aligns.
The second term computes the average parameter accuracy, where
$`|\Theta|`$ denotes the total number of ground-truth parameters
required by the target 3D tool. Each predicted parameter $`\theta_{i}`$
is scored against its ground-truth counterpart $`\theta_{i}^{*}`$ via
the similarity function $`\phi\in[0,1]`$, defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\phi(\theta_{i},\theta_{i}^{*})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\theta_{i}=\theta_{i}^{*}\\
\text{LLM-Sim}(\theta_{i},\theta_{i}^{*})&\text{if }\theta_{i},\theta_{i}^{*}~\text{are text}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
``` |  |

#### 4.3.3. Policy Optimization

To internalize the forward-looking capability derived from simulation,
we optimize the agent’s policy $`\pi`$ using the collected interaction
trajectories. We investigate two distinct paradigms to refine the
Approver’s decision boundary: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct
Preference Optimization (DPO) ([Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)).
Instead of relying on manual annotation, we leverage the automated
metrics from our simulation loop to curate training signals. For SFT, we
iteratively select top-ranked responses to build realistic,
goal-directed interaction trajectories. For DPO, we construct pairwise
comparisons by ranking responses at each turn, distinguishing “chosen”
and “rejected” pairs based on MR scores.

## 5. The 3D-Clarify Benchmark

To rigorously evaluate Clare’s capability in ambiguity resolution and
long-horizon coordination, we construct 3D-Clarify, a comprehensive
benchmark comprising 620 interaction scenarios. The construction
pipeline is automated, consisting of three phases: atomic task
generation, sequential composition, and uncertainty injection.

### 5.1. Phase 1: Atomic Task Generation

Table 1. Single-turn atomic task distribution across 3D domains and
sub-domains. The supported tools denote the current toolset integrated
into our agent, while the dataset design ensures the integration of
future tools.The table groups 500 atomic tasks by five 3D domains and

As shown in
Table [1](#acmlabel4 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1. Phase 1: Atomic Task Generation ‣ 5. The 3D-Clarify Benchmark ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration"),
we first establish a foundation of 500 single-turn atomic tasks. To
ensure robust coverage, we define parameter spaces for five canonical 3D
domains: Text-to-3D Generation, Single-View Reconstruction, Multi-View
Reconstruction, Point Cloud Editing, and Post-Processing (including
Outlier Removal and Type Conversion).

For each task $`\tau`$, we employ a template-based generation engine. We
map high-level user constraints (e.g., "high quality", "fast speed") to
specific executable parameters $`\Theta_{\tau}`$ of compatible
foundation models (e.g., Trellis, Hunyuan3D, VGGT). By procedurally
sampling valid parameter combinations and wrapping them in diverse
natural language templates, we generate ground-truth triplets
$`(q,\mathcal{G}^{*},\text{Code}^{*})`$. This ensures a rigorous mapping
where every natural language instruction $`q`$ has a verifiable goal
$`\mathcal{G}^{*}=\{p_{in},f,c,\theta\}`$ and maps to a certain tool
$`\mathcal{T}_{3D}`$ with required parameters $`\theta_{exec}`$.

Crucially, this construction methodology emphasizes generalizability. By
decoupling abstract user constraints from specific tool implementations,
our benchmark is tool-agnostic: adapting to other 3D tools
$`\mathcal{T}_{3D}^{*}`$ with similar functional properties requires
only establishing a corresponding model mapping (e.g., mapping "high
quality" to a new model’s specific high-resolution parameter) during
evaluation. This design ensures that 3D-Clarify remains a relevant
standard even as underlying foundation models upgrade.

### 5.2. Phase 2: Sequential Multi-Task Composition

Real-world 3D workflows often involve sequential dependencies. To
simulate this, we construct 120 multi-step samples by chaining atomic
tasks based on 15 distinct workflow templates (e.g., Reconstruction
$`\rightarrow`$ Editing $`\rightarrow`$ Outlier Removal). To mirror the
natural ambiguity of human communication in sequential pipelines, we
intentionally obfuscate the explicit file paths for intermediate inputs.
Rather than providing absolute paths for downstream operations, the
simulated user employs contextual co-references to denote intermediate
results. This design explicitly challenges the agent to maintain a
persistent state, requiring it to accurately resolve cross-turn
dependencies and correctly map previous outputs to subsequent inputs to
successfully execute the entire workflow.

### 5.3. Phase 3: Synthesizing Underspecified Requirements

To systematically evaluate clarification capabilities, we apply three
controlled perturbation strategies to the ground-truth goals
(Figure [3](#acmlabel3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3.1. Interactive Forward Sampling ‣ 4.3. Self-Evolution via Collaborative Simulation ‣ 4. The CLARE Framework: Coordination via Progressive Alignment ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration"))
to simulate a "Lazy User" persona. Building upon our problem
formulation, we synthesize: (1) Ambiguity Injection, where we apply
semantic bleaching via task-specific templates, replacing
domain-specific terms with generic actions and stripping parametric
constraints; (2) Missing Information, where we mask concrete execution
parameters with indefinite placeholders while retaining structural
intent; and (3) Mistaken Details, which simulate erroneous user beliefs
requiring active correction. This is achieved by injecting
contradictions, input modality mismatches (e.g., providing a 2D .jpg for
a task requiring a 3D .ply), and out-of-bound values.

## 6. Experiments

### 6.1. Experiment Setup

To rigorously evaluate the capability of agents in handling realistic
user requirements, we utilize our proposed 3D-Clarify benchmark, which
comprises 500 single-step and 120 multi-step tasks, each associated with
three underspecified queries. Diverging from single-turn paradigms, we
emphasize dynamic goal fulfillment by leveraging Qwen3-8B as a stateful
user simulator to emulate authentic, multi-turn behaviors conditioned on
the initial query, final objective, and dialogue history. Our agent
components are similarly powered by Qwen3-8B.

To enable adaptive tool orchestration, we construct a comprehensive
model knowledge base by analyzing a diverse suite of integrated 3D
toolsets, including Worldgen ([Xie, 2025](#bib.bib36)), Trellis ([Xiang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)), Triplaneturbo ([Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35)), Hunyuan-3D ([Team, 2025b](#bib.bib30); [Team,
2025a](#bib.bib31); [Team, 2024](#bib.bib32)), VGGT ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)), Fast3R ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)),
Concerto ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib28)), and Open3D ([Zhou et al.,
2018](#bib.bib27)). For self-evolution, we perform LoRA-based
fine-tuning on the Proactive Approver using a de-duplicated subset of
3,000 multi-turn trajectories filtered by the Multi-turn Reward. Both
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
are conducted using the LLaMA-Factory ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib37))
framework on two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs for 2 epochs, utilizing a learning
rate of $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ and a total batch size of 4. For a fair
comparison, all baselines employ the identical Qwen3-8B backbone. For
Clare and the original baselines, inference uses temperature $`0.6`$ and
top_p $`0.9`$; the structured-output adapters use temperature $`0.2`$
and top_p $`0.9`$, as detailed in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4. Training Details ‣ Appendix A Method Details ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration").
All interactive methods use a maximum interaction limit of $`T_{max}=8`$
turns. In the reward formulation, the penalty coefficient $`\lambda`$ is
set to $`0.1`$.

Detailed agent prompts, tool specifications, benchmark construction, and
model-selection knowledge are provided in
Appendices [A](#A1 "Appendix A Method Details ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
and [B](#A2 "Appendix B 3D Clarify Benchmark Details ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration").

### 6.2. Baselines

To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we compare
against static single-turn prompting methods (Zero-shot, Few-shot, and
Chain-of-Thought ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib8))) and dynamic,
feedback-driven agentic frameworks (ReAct ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6)) and Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib7))). We
further include three task-interface-matched related-work adapters:
CLAMBER ([Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib22)), which uses a single
clarification-aware agent; CEP ([Zhang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib25)),
which follows an ask-before-plan state collection, clarification, and
planning flow; and 3D-GPT ([Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)), which
follows task dispatch, conceptualization, and modeling. These adapters
retain their defining control flows while using the same Qwen3-8B
backbone, simulated user, 3D tool interface, turn budget, and evaluator
as Clare; they are adaptations to our executor rather than exact
reproductions. Full implementation details are provided in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1. Baseline Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Extended Experimental Results ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration").

### 6.3. Evaluation Metrics

We adopt two widely recognized metrics to evaluate agent performance on
the benchmark: Goal Completion Rate (CR), which quantifies the extent of
task fulfillment for each individual task, and Task Success Rate (SR),
which measures the ratio of tasks that are fully accomplished. For each
task, we verify: (1) Module Name: correctness of the target module
identification; (2) Prompt & Parameters: consistency of text-to-3D
prompts validated by LLM judgment, along with other generation
parameters; (3) Input File Path: existence and validity of referenced
input assets; (4) Output File Extension: correctness of naming
conventions (e.g., .glb, .obj).

Table [2](#acmlabel5 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2. Phase 2: Sequential Multi-Task Composition ‣ 5. The 3D-Clarify Benchmark ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
presents the comparison on the 3D-Clarify benchmark. We emphasize Task
Success Rate (SR) as the primary metric for flawless execution, while
Goal Completion Rate (CR) reflects partial parametric accuracy. Our
analysis yields three key findings.

##### Proactive Clarification is Essential for Underspecified Requirements.

For single-step tasks, single-turn paradigms (Zero-shot, Few-shot, CoT)
nearly collapse on ambiguity and missing-info tasks, achieving only 0–6%
SR despite moderate CR scores (31–35% and 17–18%, respectively). Dynamic
agentic frameworks (ReAct, Reflexion) show similar failures (1.6–8.4% SR
on ambiguity/missing tasks). Adding clarification-aware or 3D-specific
scaffolds improves some cases, but the best adapter reaches only 24.40%
average SR on single-step tasks and 9.44% on multi-step tasks. In
contrast, Clare-base achieves 48.60% and 27.22% average SR,
respectively. This gap indicates that an ask-first prompt or standard 3D
decomposition alone is insufficient; reliable execution also requires
explicit pre-execution gating and persistent clarified state.

##### Self-Evolution via MR Optimization Substantially Improves Clarification Policies.

Multi-turn reward optimization yields significant gains in both SR and
CR. On ambiguity single-step tasks, Clare-SE-DPO achieves 60.00% SR (CR:
70.52%) compared to Clare-base’s 45.80% SR—a 14.20% absolute
improvement. On missing-info tasks, Clare-SE-SFT reaches 52.00% SR (CR:
69.47%), while Clare-SE-DPO achieves 59.40% SR (CR: 75.32%). For
mistaken tasks, Clare-SE-SFT attains the highest 66.80% SR (CR: 85.43%).
Averaged across all single-step underspecifications, Clare-SE-DPO
achieves 60.40% SR (CR: 73.51%), more than doubling the strongest
baseline (CEP: 24.40% SR) and demonstrating that clarification policies
are learnable through simulated interaction.

##### Multi-Step Tasks Amplify the Advantage of Structured Clarification.

The transition to multi-step workflows reveals a critical finding:
baseline methods collapse to 0% SR on ambiguity and missing-info
multi-step tasks, while Clare-SE-DPO maintains 34.17–49.17% SR (CR:
53.41–68.74%). This 34–49% absolute gap underscores that multi-step
workflows require consistent clarification across turns—a capability
enabled by Clare’s Contextual Summarizer for maintaining structured task
state. On mistaken multi-step tasks, Clare-SE-SFT achieves 48.33% SR
(CR: 83.77%), demonstrating that early-stage clarification prevents
error propagation. Overall, Clare-SE-DPO attains 43.34% average SR (CR:
64.97%) on multi-step tasks, compared to 4.44–7.78% SR for dynamic
baselines and 11.39–13.89% SR for single-turn paradigms. While absolute
performance indicates room for growth (e.g., larger backbones), Clare
represents the first demonstration that proactive clarification is the
key to reliable 3D task execution under underspecified requirements.

##### Performance Analysis on Mistaken Details.

We observe a striking divergence between Goal Completion Rate (CR) and
Task Success Rate (SR) across baselines on mistaken tasks. For instance,
single-step Zero-shot achieves 77.55% CR but only 34.80% SR. Because the
underlying LLM possesses strong instruction-following capabilities,
baselines successfully configure most standard parameters, artificially
inflating CR. However, lacking proactive clarification, they blindly
execute intentionally injected fatal errors, causing the overall
execution to collapse. Conversely, our framework intercepts these
errors, though CLARE-SE-SFT outperforms CLARE-SE-DPO (66.80% vs. 61.80%
single-step SR). We attribute this to the inherent conflict between
preference alignment and error correction. SFT directly clones robust
"firm correction" trajectories via maximum likelihood estimation. In
contrast, preference optimization (DPO) biases the model toward
compliant, agreeable responses. Consequently, when confronted with
explicit user errors, the DPO agent experiences policy degradation in
the challenging action of proactively contradicting the user, leading to
lower success rates.

### 6.5. Qualitative Evaluation of 3D Execution

Figure [4](#acmlabel6 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.4. Quantitative Results ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
visualizes Clare’s robustness across three underspecification scenarios:
Overcoming Blind Execution: Baselines hallucinate parameters for
ambiguous requests (e.g., a generic frog), whereas CLARE clarifies the
target ("blue poison-dart frog"). Bridging Information Gaps: Baselines
fatally crash by executing placeholder code or selecting default tools.
CLARE proactively queries missing parameters (e.g., image paths) prior
to invocation. Preempting Failures: Baselines pass invalid parameters
causing API crashes. CLARE identifies constraint violations
pre-execution, confirming proactive gating outperforms post-hoc
recovery.

### 6.6. Interaction Efficiency Analysis

Two dual-axis plots compare five methods on single-step and multi-step
tasks, using bars for average interaction turns and orange lines for
success rate. CLARE variants use roughly 2.7--3.7 turns and achieve
27.2--60.4 percent success, substantially above ReAct and Reflexion at
about 1.2--1.5 turns and 4.4--16.1 percent, with DPO highest in both
settings.

illustrates the trade-off between interaction cost and task performance.
ReAct and Reflexion require only 1.34–1.51 turns on single-step tasks,
but achieve SRs of merely 7.8% and 16.1%, respectively. In contrast,
Clare-base uses 3.65 turns to reach 48.6% SR on single-step tasks and
2.69 turns to reach 27.2% SR on multi-step tasks. MR optimization adds
only 0.07 and 0.76 turns for Clare-SE-DPO, while increasing SR to 60.4%
and 43.3%, respectively. These results show that strategic clarification
substantially improves task completion at a modest interaction cost.

To quantify the contribution of individual modules within Clare, we
conduct ablation studies by disabling the Proactive Approver and the
Contextual Summarizer.

reports the results.

Table 3. Ablation study on 3D-Clarify’s single-step and multi-step
tasks. Results are averaged across three types of underspecification
(Ambiguity, Missing, Mistaken).Rows compare CLARE-base with variants
that remove the Summarizer or Approver, and columns report completion
and success rates on single-step and multi-step tasks. Removing the
Approver causes the largest decline, reducing success rate from 48.60 to
27.67 on single-step tasks and from 27.22 to 13.06 on multi-step tasks.

Removing the Approver causes the most severe performance degradation: on
single-step tasks, SR drops from 48.60% to 27.67% (-20.93% absolute),
and CR falls from 66.26% to 52.04% (-14.22%). On multi-step tasks, the
SR decline is also substantial (from 27.22% to 13.06%, -14.16%). This
validates our central hypothesis: the ability to detect ambiguity,
missing information, and mistaken details before execution is the
foundation of Clare’s effectiveness. Without this gating mechanism, the
system reverts to blind execution, hallucinating parameters and failing
to resolve information gaps.

The Summarizer exhibits complexity-dependent utility. While its impact
on single-step tasks is negligible ($`\Delta`$SR: -0.40%), its absence
significantly impairs multi-step workflows, where SR drops by 6.94% and
CR by 7.41%. This divergence validates our design rationale: while the
Summarizer is redundant for atomic instructions, it is indispensable for
maintaining structured state and resolving cross-turn dependencies as
interaction depth increases.

### 6.8. Effect of Training Data Scale

We investigate the impact of training data scale on self-evolution
performance across 120 multi-step tasks. As illustrated by the learning
curves in
Figure [6](#acmlabel9 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.8. Effect of Training Data Scale ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration"),
SFT and DPO exhibit distinct scaling behaviors. SFT demonstrates rapid
initial convergence with diminishing returns: Success Rate (SR) surges
by 7.22% (from 34.17% to 41.39%) when scaling from 1,000 to 2,000
samples, but plateaus at 3,000 (42.22%). Conversely, while DPO’s
Completion Rate (CR) gains are marginal, its SR trajectory shows
superior scalability, ultimately reaching 43.34% at 3,000 and
outperforming SFT. This divergence suggests that preference-based
optimization excels at refining the decision boundary for task success
even after parametric learning saturates. Consequently, while 2,000
samples provide a cost-effective equilibrium for SFT, DPO requires
larger datasets ($`\geq`$3,000) to fully manifest its advantages in
decision-quality optimization.

A line chart plots completion rate as dashed lines and success rate as
solid lines for SFT and DPO as the training set grows from 0 to 3,000
samples. Completion rates rise from 53.38 percent to 67.20 percent for
SFT and 64.97 percent for DPO, while success rates rise from 27.22
percent to 42.22 percent and 43.34 percent, respectively, with DPO
overtaking SFT in success rate at 3,000 samples.

## 7. Conclusion

We present Clare, a self-evolving, clarify-before-execute multi-agent
framework that resolves underspecified requirements in 3D tool
orchestration, together with the 620-task, five-domain 3D-Clarify
benchmark. Across static prompting, dynamic agentic methods, and
task-interface-matched CLAMBER, CEP, and 3D-GPT adapters, Clare
consistently improves execution reliability by clarifying ambiguity,
missing information, and mistaken constraints before tool use. Its
MR-optimized policy reaches 60.40% SR on 500 single-step tasks and
43.34% SR on 120 multi-step tasks, more than doubling the strongest
baseline on single-step tasks. These results show that proactive
clarification policies can be learned and optimized through simulated
multi-turn interaction, offering a practical path toward more reliable
human–AI collaboration in specification-heavy 3D workflows.

##### Limitations.

The overall execution success of Clare is inherently bounded by the
capabilities of the backbone LLM and the integrated 3D toolchains.
Additionally, while our simulated environment effectively optimizes
clarification policies, fully capturing the diversity and
unpredictability of real-world human queries remains an ongoing
challenge.

## Appendix A Method Details

### A.1. Architecture

To effectively manage the uncertainty of human intent, CLARE employs a
multi-agent progressive alignment loop that decouples the 3D generation
pipeline into four specialized cognitive roles. This collaborative
architecture ensures that requirements are fully specified before
invoking computationally expensive 3D tools.

- •
  Proactive Approver (Cognitive Gatekeeper): Acting as the first line of
  defense, the Approver evaluates the completeness of the user’s current
  instruction against the multi-turn conversation history. Instead of
  defaulting to blind execution, it computes a binary decision state to
  detect ambiguity, missing information, or mistaken details. The
  Approver outputs its decision in a strict XML format (\<judgement\>
  and \<reason\>), effectively freezing the execution pipeline and
  categorizing the rejection (e.g., unclear objectives, invalid file
  paths) until the user’s intent becomes fully actionable.
- •
  Contextual Summarizer (Structured Intent Mining): Once a request is
  approved, the Summarizer acts as the system’s dynamic memory by
  aggregating fragmented multi-turn dialogue into a normalized task
  manifest. It performs essential state tracking and co-reference
  resolution. The output is strictly formatted into XML fields
  (\<task_type\>, \<task_summary\>, \<file_path\>, and \<extra_info\>),
  which distills noisy conversational context into explicit execution
  constraints and provides a noise-free specification for the downstream
  code synthesis.
- •
  3D-Aware Programmer (Adaptive Tool Orchestration): The Programmer is
  responsible for translating the structured manifest into executable
  Python code. Unlike generic code generators, it incorporates a
  built-in Model Selection Knowledge Base to understand the capability
  boundaries and input/output formats of different 3D tools. It
  dynamically maps user-defined constraints (such as speed and quality)
  to specific models $`\mathcal{T}_{3D}`$ and execution parameters
  $`\theta_{exec}`$. This ensures that the synthesized code is not only
  syntactically correct but also physically and semantically grounded in
  the 3D generation context.
- •
  Interaction Feedback Provider (Closing the Semantic Gap): This module
  serves as the interface for conversational alignment, translating
  internal system states into human-readable, actionable feedback. It
  operates in two adaptive modes. In Clarification Mode, it intercepts
  the Approver’s rejection reasoning and translates it into targeted
  follow-up questions, guiding the user to provide missing parameters
  without cognitive overload. In Status Reporting Mode, it interprets
  raw execution logs and potential runtime errors post-execution,
  providing the user with concise summaries and clear next-step
  suggestions to iteratively refine their 3D assets.

### A.2. Details and Prompts of CLARE Agents

#### A.2.1. Proactive Approver

The Approver is the core role responsible for "decision gating." In each
round of dialogue, it receives the current user input and the existing
dialogue history, combines them into a complete requirement, and then
determines whether the requirement meets the "executable" condition.
"Executable" means that the requirement must contain a clear task
objective (four types of 3D workflows), corresponding input information
(such as image file paths or text prompts), and necessary parameters and
output format. In addition, for generation/reconstruction classes, a
clear output format is required (such as .ply/.glb), for post-processing
classes, specific operations are required (such as removing
outliers/converting meshes to point clouds), and for point cloud editing
classes, the "detail objects" to be edited are required (such as "remove
chair/keep table"). When the task is sufficiently specific, Approver
must output strict XML: ‘\<judgement\> Yes\</judgement\>‘. If the task
still contains missing, ambiguous, or erroneous elements, it must output
‘\<judgement\> No\</judgement\>‘ along with a ‘\<reason\>‘ in the same
output, where the reason is selected from predefined rejection
categories (Missing information / Task objective unclear / Mistaken
details / User wants to clarify or confirm the task details).
Furthermore, Approver’s output is protocolized to a format that "must
contain only these XML tags," ensuring stable and reliable routing.
Assistants, as the core of the Agent framework, support the use of
trained preference models (e.g., via DPO/SFT), allowing them to directly
influence the quality of gating decisions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.2.2. Contextual Summarizer

Once the Approver determines that the current dialogue is sufficiently
specific, the system calls the Summarizer to compress the multi-turn
dialogue into an "executable, structured task description." This summary
is output in strict XML format and contains four fixed fields:
‘task_type‘ (supporting combinations such as
reconstruction/generation/post-processing/point cloud editing),
‘task_summary‘ (breaking down the requirements into concise steps and
describing the output format of each step), ‘file_path‘ (a set of
user-provided input paths), and ‘extra_info‘ (execution-related
parameters and preference information, such as
quality/speed/style/output format). This structured summary is then
packaged as input and passed to the Programmer to generate the final
executable code.

\<task_type\> Multi-View 3D Reconstruction \</task_type\>
\<task_summary\> Perform multi-view 3D reconstruction using
./data/source/multiview/scene/Auditorium as the input source based on
constraints \</task_summary\> \<file_path\>
./data/source/multiview/scene/Auditorium \</file_path\> \<extra_info\>
Constraints: \[speed: Fast speed\]; Output Path:
./outputs/Auditorium.ply \</extra_info\>

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.2.3. 3D-Aware Programmer

After receiving the structured task summary, the Programmer first parses
the task type and retrieves candidate model information matching the
current task type from the built-in Model Selection Knowledge Base. It
then injects the output format and capability features of these models
as priors for model selection into the prompts, constraining the LLM to
follow correct tool selection and parameter constraints when generating
code. Subsequently, it generates a directly executable Python code call
sequence according to preset template rules, and performs
post-processing with regularization to correct key call forms, thereby
improving the executability of the generated code and its consistency
with downstream 3D tool interfaces.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.2.4. Interaction Feedback Provider

The Feedback Provider is responsible for translating internal states
into user-facing next-step instructions. When subsequent code execution
successfully triggers the system to the ‘success‘ state, it provides a
brief confirmation and summary to the user based on the input details of
the current task and the output location of the generated/executed
results, and offers possible next-step suggestions if necessary (e.g.,
whether further processing or editing is required). Conversely, when the
system is in the ‘failed‘ state triggered by code execution failure, it
identifies the most likely point of error based on the provided error
details and the reason for the failure, and provides actionable
corrective directions. This helps the user clarify what information
needs to be supplemented or which parameters/constraints need to be
adjusted, allowing the conversation to quickly return to a recoverable
track and continue converging after a failure.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.3. Tools

We provide a comprehensive suite of 3D processing tools to support
diverse agent workflows. Each tool is integrated into the system with
specific input/output constraints and functional roles as detailed
below:

##### Trellis

([Xiang et al., 2024](#bib.bib33))

- •
  Core Capability: High-quality 3D generation and reconstruction
  featuring high-fidelity mesh output.
- •
  System Role: Serving as the primary model for Text to 3D Generation
  and 3D Reconstruction.
- •
  I/O: Supports Text/Image as input and exports to .ply, .obj, or .glb
  formats.

##### TriplaneTurbo

([Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib35))

- •
  Core Capability: Lightweight and fast-speed text-to-3D generation.
- •
  System Role: As a lightweight Text to 3D Generation model.
- •
  I/O: Processes Text prompts into .obj mesh files.

##### WorldGen

([Xie, 2025](#bib.bib36))

- •
  Core Capability: Specialized in scene-level 3D generation with
  detailed geometry.
- •
  System Role: Handles complex environment generation tasks.
- •
  I/O: Supports Text input and outputs .ply, .obj, .glb, or .stl.

##### VGGT

([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib29))

- •
  Core Capability: Dense 3D reconstruction optimized for both objects
  and scenes.
- •
  System Role: Provides fast-speed 3D Reconstruction from single or
  multiple view inputs, typically producing dense point clouds.
- •
  I/O: Accepts Images and generates .ply or .glb files.

##### Hunyuan-3D

([Team, 2025b](#bib.bib30); [Team, 2025a](#bib.bib31); [Team,
2024](#bib.bib32))

- •
  Core Capability: Ultra-high quality single-view reconstruction with
  detailed mesh geometry.
- •
  System Role: Used for high-precision object digitizing tasks where
  processing speed is less critical than surface accuracy.
- •
  I/O: Converts a single Image into .glb or .obj formats.

##### Fast3R

([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib34))

- •
  Core Capability: Extreme-speed multi-view reconstruction using
  lightweight point cloud representations.
- •
  System Role: Designed for real-time or low-resource scenarios
  requiring efficient scene reconstruction.
- •
  I/O: Processes Multi-view Images into .ply point clouds.

##### Concerto

([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib28))

- •
  Core Capability: Enables semantic editing of indoor point clouds,
  including object segmentation, deletion, or retention.
- •
  System Role: Used for point cloud editing.
- •
  I/O: Processes .ply point clouds into .ply point clouds.

##### Open3D

([Zhou et al., 2018](#bib.bib27))

- •
  Outlier Removal: Statistically cleans noise from raw point clouds to
  improve downstream quality; supports .ply I/O.
- •
  Mesh2PCD: Provides geometric conversion by sampling discrete point
  clouds from mesh surfaces (.obj/.glb to .ply).

### A.4. Training Details

#### A.4.1. Interactive Forward Sampling

To estimate the long-term utility of a clarification strategy, Clare
performs forward lookahead via simulation. Given a context
$`x=(q_{j},\mathcal{H}_{<j})`$, the agent samples $`N`$ candidate
responses $`\{m^{(1)},\dots,m^{(N)}\}`$ from its current policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$. For each candidate, we roll out a full interaction
trajectory $`\tau^{(i)}`$ by coupling the agent with a Simulated User
$`\mathcal{U}`$. This process reveals downstream consequences, helping
the agent separate vital clarifications from redundant, costly queries.
Below, we detail the specific implementation of this simulation loop.

##### Candidate Generation and Deduplication

At each step, the Proactive Approver evaluates the completeness of the
user instruction. To encourage exploration of diverse clarification
strategies, we sample $`N=8`$ candidates from the policy using a high
temperature ($`T=1.0`$). Each candidate implies a binary decision state
$`d\in\{\text{EXECUTE},\text{CLARIFY}\}`$, alongside a corresponding
reasoning trace. To optimize computational efficiency during the rollout
phase, we apply a deduplication mechanism based on a content hash of the
parsed decision and reasoning. Only unique candidates are retained for
full trajectory rollouts, avoiding redundant simulations of identical
strategies.

##### Trajectory Rollout via Multi-Role Simulation

For each unique candidate, we roll out an interaction trajectory
$`\tau`$ that can span up to a maximum limit of $`T_{max}=8`$ turns. The
state transitions depend on the Approver’s decision state $`d`$:

- •
  Clarification Branch ($`d=\text{CLARIFY}`$): The Interaction Feedback
  Provider translates the Approver’s reasoning into a targeted
  clarification question. The Simulated User $`\mathcal{U}`$-which holds
  the ground-truth goal $`\mathcal{G}^{*}=\{p_{in},f,c,\theta\}`$ and
  operates under a strict information asymmetry setting-provides a
  response based on its current behavioral stage. This refined input is
  appended to the dialogue history, and the agent is queried again in
  the next turn.
- •
  Execution Branch ($`d=\text{EXECUTE}`$): The clarification loop
  breaks. The Contextual Summarizer aggregates the multi-turn dialogue
  history into a normalized task manifest $`\mathcal{M}`$. This manifest
  is passed to the 3D-Aware Programmer, which maps the constraints to
  specific 3D tools $`\mathcal{T}_{3D}`$ and parameters
  $`\theta_{exec}`$ to synthesize executable Python code.

##### Multi-turn Reward Evaluation and Back-propagation

Upon trajectory termination (either via code execution or reaching
$`T_{max}`$), an automated verifier evaluates the final output. Rather
than a simple binary outcome, we compute a continuous Multi-turn Reward
(MR) that balances task fidelity against interaction efficiency:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
MR(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(\text{Exec}(\mathcal{T}_{3D},\theta_{exec}),\mathcal{G}^{*})-\lambda\cdot K
``` |  |

where $`K`$ is the number of interaction turns and $`\lambda`$ is a
penalty coefficient (set to $`0.1`$) to discourage verbosity. The value
function $`\mathcal{V}\in[0,1]`$ enforces strict parametric accuracy by
checking both module alignment and specific parameter similarities
against the latent goal $`\mathcal{G}^{*}`$.

Because intermediate clarification turns do not yield immediate
functional 3D outputs, we employ outcome reward back-propagation: the
final trajectory reward $`MR(\tau)`$ is retroactively mapped to all
step-level instruction-output pairs within that specific trajectory
$`\tau`$. This mechanism ensures that early, proactive questions are
correctly credited for enabling successful downstream execution,
providing dense preference signals for subsequent Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

#### A.4.2. Self-Evolution Training Details

To implement the self-evolution policy optimization described in Section
\[Insert Main Section Reference\], we utilize the LLaMA-Factory
framework to train the Proactive Approver. Both the Supervised
Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) stages share
a foundational setup, initialized from the Qwen3-8B backbone.

##### Shared Hyperparameters

To achieve memory-efficient training on our hardware setup (two NVIDIA
RTX 3090 GPUs), we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with a rank of
$`r=16`$, targeting all linear modules (lora_target: all). Both SFT and
DPO are trained for 2 epochs using a peak learning rate of
$`5.0\times 10^{-6}`$ with a cosine learning rate scheduler and a warmup
ratio of $`0.1`$. We use a per-device batch size of 2 with no gradient
accumulation, resulting in an effective total batch size of 4 across the
two GPUs. All training is conducted using bfloat16 mixed precision and a
maximum sequence length (cutoff length) of 2048 tokens to accommodate
the multi-turn conversational history.

##### Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) Setup

For the SFT phase, we fine-tune the agent on a curated dataset of
approximately 3,000 high-quality trajectories (filtered by Multi-turn
Reward). To optimize GPU memory and computation, this stage utilizes
DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2 optimization. The objective here is to clone the
behavior of the top-ranked clarification trajectories via standard
maximum likelihood estimation.

##### Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Setup

For the DPO phase, the dataset consists of approximately 3,000 pairwise
comparisons constructed from the simulated rollouts, where "chosen" and
"rejected" trajectories are distinguished based on their composite
Multi-turn Reward. We employ the standard Sigmoid preference loss. The
KL divergence penalty coefficient is set to $`\beta=0.1`$ to prevent the
model from deviating too far from the reference policy. Because DPO
requires maintaining both the active policy model and a frozen reference
model in memory simultaneously, we scale our memory optimization by
utilizing DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 for this phase.

### B.1. System Prompts for Simulated User

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2. Detailed Task Scenarios

![An overview of the proposed task scenario](2607.16352v1/ds_ap.png)

Figure 7. Comprehensive overview of detailed single-turn atomic task
scenarios across diverse 3D domains and sub-domains, demonstrating the
performance of the proposed CLARE framework. For each task, we present
the user input prompt, the input file(if any), and the high-quality 3D
output generated by CLARE, showcasing its capability to handle diverse,
fine-grained 3D requirements with natural language instructions.An
overview of the proposed task scenario

As shown in
Figure [7](#acmlabel10 "Figure 7 ‣ B.2. Detailed Task Scenarios ‣ Appendix B 3D Clarify Benchmark Details ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration"),
we design detailed task scenarios which are systematically categorized
into five primary domains, each with corresponding sub-domains:

1.  (1)
    Text-to-3D Generation: This domain focuses on generating 3D assets
    from text descriptions, and is further divided into two sub-domains:
    Scene (generating 3D scenes) and Object (generating 3D objects).
2.  (2)
    Single-View Reconstruction: This domain involves reconstructing 3D
    assets from a single 2D image input, with sub-domains including
    Scene (reconstructing 3D scenes from one view) and Object
    (reconstructing 3D objects from one view).
3.  (3)
    Multi-View Reconstruction: This domain reconstructs 3D assets from
    multiple 2D images captured from different viewpoints, with
    sub-domains of Scene (reconstructing 3D scenes from multi-view
    images) and Object (reconstructing 3D objects from multi-view
    images).
4.  (4)
    Point Cloud Editing: This domain covers operations on 3D point cloud
    data, with three sub-domains: Keeping (retaining specific point
    cloud regions), Deletion (removing unwanted point cloud data), and
    Segmentation (partitioning point clouds into semantic or
    instance-level regions).
5.  (5)
    Post-Processing: This domain focuses on refining 3D data after
    initial generation or reconstruction, with sub-domains including
    Mesh to PointCloud (converting mesh to point cloud) and Outlier
    Removal (eliminating noisy or erroneous points from 3D assets).

### B.3. Data Curation and Source Assets

To support a rigorous and comprehensive evaluation of 3D agent
capabilities under both atomic and compositional settings, we construct
a curated benchmark consisting of two subsets: a single-step set with
500 samples and a multi-step set with 120 samples. Both subsets are
designed to uniformly cover five canonical 3D task domains: text-to-3D
generation, single-view reconstruction, multi-view reconstruction, point
cloud editing, and post-processing. This design follows a
domain-balanced construction principle to ensure that agent performance
is evaluated across diverse yet representative 3D workflows.

##### Single-Step Task Construction.

We first construct a set of 500 atomic tasks, where each task
corresponds to a single executable operation without intermediate
dependency. To ensure balanced coverage, we allocate 100 samples to each
of the five task domains. Each sample is instantiated as a structured
triplet consisting of input specification, target goal, and
corresponding asset reference, enabling deterministic evaluation of
execution correctness.

##### Multi-Step Task Construction.

To simulate realistic 3D workflows that involve sequential dependencies,
we further construct 120 multi-step samples by composing multiple atomic
tasks. These compositions span cross-domain pipelines (e.g.,
reconstruction $`\rightarrow`$ editing $`\rightarrow`$ post-processing),
requiring the agent to maintain consistent state and intermediate
representations across steps. Compared to single-step tasks, these
samples emphasize long-horizon reasoning and inter-task coordination.

##### Text-to-3D Generation.

For the text-to-3D generation domain, we adopt data from the
TriplaneTurbo ([Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)) dataset. This dataset
provides high-quality text prompts. We select samples with diverse
semantic categories and varying levels of geometric complexity to ensure
broad coverage.

##### Reconstruction Tasks.

We consider both single-view and multi-view reconstruction under two
distinct settings: object-level and scene-level reconstruction.

- •
  Object-level reconstruction is based on the DTU ([Jensen et al.,
  2014](#bib.bib38)) dataset, which provides calibrated multi-view
  images and ground-truth geometry for precise object reconstruction.
- •
  Scene-level reconstruction utilizes data from Mip-NeRF 360 ([Barron et
  al., 2022](#bib.bib39)) and Tanks and Temples ([Knapitsch et al.,
  2017](#bib.bib40)), both of which contain large-scale real-world
  scenes with complex geometry and viewpoint distributions.

##### Point Cloud Editing.

For point cloud editing tasks, we source data from the ScanNet ([Dai et
al., 2017](#bib.bib41)) dataset, enabling evaluation of editing
operations such as keeping, segmentation, and deletion.

##### Post-Processing.

The post-processing tasks are constructed using a combination of
real-world and synthetic assets. Specifically, we utilize ScanNet ([Dai
et al., 2017](#bib.bib41)) data together with internally created assets
in multiple formats. This diverse set of representations enables
systematic evaluation of downstream operations, such as format
conversion and outlier removal across heterogeneous 3D data formats.

### B.4. Injection Details

The core contribution of 3D-Clarify is the controlled injection of user
uncertainty. We apply three distinct perturbation strategies to the
ground-truth goals, creating a "Lazy User" persona that tests the
agent’s ability.

##### Ambiguity Injection (Semantic & Referential Vagueness):

We simulate user uncertainty via a obfuscation strategy using
task-specific templates. We apply semantic bleaching by replacing
domain-specific verbs with generic actions and specific targets with
abstract nouns, while stripping all parametric constraints to force
context-based inference.

##### Missing Information (Value Masking):

We simulate user negligence through a template-based value masking
strategy. We replace concrete execution parameters with indefinite
placeholders while retaining the structural intent. This compels the
agent to detect that while the necessary parameter keys are mentioned,
their executable values are absent, necessitating targeted
clarification.

##### Mistaken Details (Constraint Violations):

Unlike simple missing info, these samples simulate erroneous user
beliefs that require correction rather than just filling. We synthesize
three sub-categories of mistakes:

1.  (1)
    Contextual Contradiction: We inject conflicting attributes where the
    user demands properties that are mutually exclusive for the
    underlying model.
2.  (2)
    Input Modality Mismatch: We alter input file extensions to simulate
    modality errors, such as providing a 2D image (.jpg) for a Point
    Cloud Editing task (which strictly requires 3D .ply input), forcing
    the agent to check file type compatibility.
3.  (3)
    Invalid Parameter Values: We corrupt numerical fields with
    out-of-bound or nonsensical values. This tests the agent’s ability
    to validate arguments against API constraints before execution.

## Appendix C Extended Experimental Results

### C.1. Baseline Implementation Details

In this section, we detail the implementation of the baseline methods
evaluated in our benchmark. To ensure a fair and rigorous comparison,
the static single-turn baselines-namely Zero-shot, Few-shot, and
Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-are implemented by directly adapting the system
prompt of our 3D-Aware Programmer. These baselines are instructed to act
as direct code synthesizers, translating the initial (and often
underspecified) user query straight into executable 3D tool
orchestration code without any multi-turn gating or clarification
mechanisms. For the Few-shot and CoT implementations, we augment the
base prompt with representative in-context examples and step-by-step
reasoning demonstrations, respectively.

Conversely, to evaluate the inherent multi-turn capabilities of
general-purpose agentic frameworks, we configure ReAct and Reflexion
with a dynamic, conversational action space. Specifically, we explicitly
define an interaction action alongside the generation action. This
design theoretically empowers these agents to pause execution and query
the user when they encounter ambiguous or missing information.
Furthermore, Reflexion is integrated with an execution feedback loop,
allowing it to reflect on tool execution crashes or runtime errors and
adjust its subsequent decisions.

#### C.1.1. ZeroShot

For the Zero-shot baseline, we configure the language model to act
purely as a direct instruction-to-code translator, completely bypassing
the multi-agent gating and clarification modules. The prompt defines the
agent as a "Programmer" that must map the raw, potentially
underspecified user input directly into executable Python code.
Crucially, to enforce a strict single-turn execution paradigm, the
prompt explicitly forbids conversational output or reasoning traces.
When confronted with missing information, rather than seeking
clarification, the model is instructed by the prompt to heuristically
resolve the gaps—such as deriving missing output file paths by
"slugifying" the user’s text prompt or falling back to default formats.
This implementation directly simulates the "blind execution"
vulnerability common in traditional 3D generation pipelines.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.1.2. FewShot

Building upon the zero-shot implementation, the Few-Shot baseline
introduces in-context learning to the 3D-Aware Programmer. We augment
the system prompt with a curated set of representative input-output
examples, demonstrating how to map various natural language constraints
(e.g., "high quality," "fast generation speed") to the correct 3D
foundation models (such as trellis or vggt) and API parameters. While
these demonstrations improve the language model’s syntactical formatting
and prior alignment, the framework still operates under a strict
single-turn assumption. Without the multi-agent gating and interaction
feedback mechanisms present in CLARE, this baseline remains structurally
incapable of pausing to question the user. Consequently, when faced with
genuine ambiguity or missing information, it still defaults to blind
execution and heuristic guesswork.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.1.3. CoT

To evaluate whether explicit reasoning mitigates the effects of
underspecified requirements, we implement a Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
baseline. We modify the Few-Shot prompt to mandate a structured
reasoning phase prior to code synthesis. Specifically, the model is
instructed to generate a \<plan\> that systematically analyzes the task
type, input parameters, output paths, and explicitly justifies its model
selection by mapping user constraints (e.g., quality and speed) to the
tool’s feature set. While this step-by-step deduction improves internal
logical consistency and helps the agent accurately select tools when
requirements are fully specified, it fundamentally remains a single-turn
paradigm. When critical information is absent or ambiguous, the CoT
agent attempts to "reason" its way out of the uncertainty using the same
hardcoded heuristics (such as path slugification and format overriding)
rather than pausing to elicit missing facts. Consequently, it still
succumbs to the fatal errors of blind execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.1.4. ReAct

Transitioning from static paradigms to dynamic agentic frameworks, we
implement the ReAct baseline to evaluate general-purpose iterative
reasoning. In this setup, the language model is prompted to interleave
reasoning traces (Thought) with specific task executions (Action) based
on the current context (Observation). Crucially, to provide a fair
comparison against our clarification-aware framework, we explicitly
expand the ReAct agent’s action space to include a Clarify action
alongside the standard Generate command. This design theoretically
empowers the agent to pause the execution pipeline and interrogate the
user when it detects missing information, ambiguity, or mistaken
details. However, as demonstrated in our quantitative results, without a
decoupled, rigorous gating mechanism (like CLARE’s Proactive Approver)
and specialized multi-turn interaction training, the general-purpose
ReAct agent often struggles to determine the optimal boundary between
reasoning and asking, frequently underutilizing the clarification action
and defaulting back to premature execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.1.5. Reflexion

Furthermore, Reflexion introduces an episodic memory buffer for
self-reflection. When the agent’s generated code fails to execute or
violates constraints, an automated verifier provides specific error
reasons. The agent then executes a self_reflect function to synthesize
actionable lessons (e.g., "I should…"), which are subsequently injected
into its system prompt for the next trial. While this enables the agent
to learn from its mistakes over multiple attempts (up to 3 trials in our
setup), it fundamentally relies on post-execution recovery rather than
pre-execution prevention. As demonstrated in our evaluation, this
trial-and-error approach is less efficient and less robust than CLARE’s
proactive clarification mechanism, particularly when dealing with fatal
modality mismatches or unrecoverable parameter errors that could have
been prevented prior to tool invocation.

### C.2. Experiment Details

#### C.2.1. Ablation details

We present detailed ablation results across the three underspecified
requirement types (Ambiguity, Missing Info, Mistaken) for both
single-step and multi-step tasks.
Table [2](#acmlabel5 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2. Phase 2: Sequential Multi-Task Composition ‣ 5. The 3D-Clarify Benchmark ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
in the main paper summarizes averaged results, while
Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.2.1. Ablation details ‣ C.2. Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C Extended Experimental Results ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
provides fine-grained results for each task complexity and uncertainty
type.

We evaluate two ablation variants. In w/o Summarizer, the Contextual
Summarizer is disabled and the agent operates with raw dialogue history
without structured state maintenance. In w/o Approver, the Proactive
Approver is completely removed, reducing the system to blind execution
equivalent to ReAct. Both variants retain the identical Qwen3-8B
backbone and inference configuration as Clare-base for fair comparison.

Removing the Proactive Approver causes catastrophic performance
degradation, validating that pre-execution gating is the foundation of
clarification capability. On single-step tasks, average SR drops from
48.60% to 27.67% (-20.93%). Breaking down by task type, the decline is
most severe on Missing Info tasks (41.00% to 16.20%, -24.80%),
confirming that placeholder detection fundamentally requires
pre-execution validation. Ambiguity tasks show similar degradation
(45.80% to 22.60%, -23.20%), as semantic vagueness goes unresolved
without explicit detection. Mistaken tasks exhibit the smallest decline
(59.00% to 44.20%, -14.80%), since some contradictions can still be
caught via runtime errors. On multi-step tasks, degradation intensifies:
average SR drops from 27.22% to 13.06% (-14.16%), with Missing Info
collapsing to merely 0.83%, demonstrating that multi-turn information
gaps become nearly impossible to resolve without proactive detection.

The Contextual Summarizer exhibits clear complexity-dependent utility,
with negligible impact on single-step tasks but substantial contribution
to multi-step workflows. On single-step tasks, removal causes minimal
degradation (48.60% to 48.20%, -0.40%), confirming that atomic
instructions require no structured state. However, on multi-step tasks,
the impact becomes pronounced: average SR drops from 27.22% to 20.28%
(-6.94%). Ambiguity proves most sensitive (23.33% to 6.67%, -16.66%), as
multi-turn semantic resolution demands persistent tracking of clarified
constraints. Interestingly, Missing Info shows slight improvement
(22.50% to 25.83%, +3.33%), suggesting that for certain
missing-information patterns, raw dialogue history may preserve richer
contextual cues than summarized state. Mistaken tasks show moderate
decline (35.83% to 28.33%, -7.50%), indicating cross-turn contradiction
detection benefits from structured representation.

These findings reveal distinct task-type-specific vulnerabilities and
inform targeted improvements. The Approver’s dominant contribution
suggests prioritizing its enhancement through more sophisticated
detection mechanisms or domain-specific validators. The Summarizer’s
complexity-dependent utility motivates adaptive designs: lightweight
summarization for single-turn queries and full structured state for
multi-turn workflows. The resilience of Mistaken tasks supports hybrid
detection combining pre-execution validation with post-execution error
analysis. Together, the ablation study validates our modular
architecture where the Approver provides essential gating and the
Summarizer enables scalable multi-turn coordination.
````
