### C.3. Statistical Analysis of Failure Modes

Figure 8. Distribution of failure reasons across three underspecified
requirement types on Clare-SE-DPO. Each group shows the count of five
error categories for Ambiguous, Missing Info, and Mistaken tasks. The
distinct error profiles reveal task-type-specific vulnerabilities.

Figure [8](#A3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ C.3. Statistical Analysis of Failure Modes ‣ Appendix C Extended Experimental Results ‣ Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration")
visualizes the failure reason distribution across the three
underspecified requirement types. Several patterns emerge:

##### Ambiguous Tasks: Dominated by Stuck Errors.

Ambiguous queries exhibit the highest stuck rate (88 occurrences, 41.7%
of ambiguous failures). This aligns with the nature of semantic
vagueness: when user requests lack concrete targets (e.g., “create
something”), agents struggle to terminate clarification and commit to
execution. The second most common failure is model selection (52
occurrences, 24.6%), suggesting that even after clarification, agents
often misinfer the appropriate foundation model from underspecified
semantic cues.

##### Missing Info Tasks: Input Path Validation Failures.

Missing information queries show a distinctive spike in input_path
errors (69 occurrences, 32.7%), followed by model errors (60
occurrences, 28.4%). This pattern reflects the structural nature of
missing-info perturbations: when parameter values are masked with
placeholders, agents frequently fail to resolve input file dependencies,
leading to execution failures. The high model error rate indicates that
path resolution and model selection are coupled challenges in
underspecified scenarios.

##### Mistaken Tasks: Parameter and Stuck Errors.

Mistaken detail queries exhibit a bimodal distribution: parameter errors
(63 occurrences, 32.6%) and stuck errors (63 occurrences, 32.6%)
dominate equally. This reflects the dual challenge of handling
contradictory constraints: agents either attempt to execute with invalid
parameters (e.g., incompatible file formats, out-of-bound values) or
become trapped in clarification loops when attempting to resolve
unresolvable contradictions. The lower model error rate (35 occurrences,
18.1%) suggests that mistaken tasks often provide sufficient semantic
grounding for model selection, even when other parameters are erroneous.

### C.4. Failure Case Analysis

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Semantic Misalignment in Model Selection

While the framework demonstrates robust capabilities in resolving
explicit parameter uncertainties, qualitative analysis reveals edge
cases where semantic misunderstandings lead to suboptimal tool
orchestration. The following case study illustrates a scenario where the
system successfully resolves syntactic ambiguity but fails at semantic
scale inference.

##### Interaction Summary

The interaction begins with a severely underspecified user prompt:
"Create something." The Proactive Approver correctly intercepts this
request, refusing blind execution and triggering a four-turn
clarification dialogue. Through this proactive questioning, the agent
successfully elicits the target entity ("Westminster Abbey"), an
aesthetic preference ("style of a DSLR photo"), and the explicit output
path and format ("./outputs/Westminster_Abbey.obj"). With these
constraints fulfilled, the Contextual Summarizer formulates a complete
task manifest, and the Programmer successfully generates executable code
without triggering any runtime errors.

Point of Failure Despite the flawless interaction flow and crash-free
execution, the orchestration ultimately results in a semantic failure
during the tool selection phase. The Programmer synthesizes the
following execution code:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

According to the system’s defined Model Selection Knowledge Base, the
triplaneturbo model is explicitly engineered for lightweight,
single-object generation. Conversely, Westminster Abbey is a massive
architectural landmark that strictly dictates a scene-level generation
pipeline (e.g., worldgen).

##### Analysis and Takeaway

This failure highlights a critical limitation in the agent’s spatial and
common-sense reasoning. While the system efficiently gathers explicit
constraints (format, style, file path), the Programmer fails to
implicitly deduce the physical scale and domain of the requested entity.
Because the user requested a "3D model of a famous landmark" rather than
explicitly utilizing the keyword "scene," the agent defaulted to an
object-centric foundation model.

This case underscores the necessity for future iterations of 3D agents
to incorporate more rigorous semantic scale validation. It demonstrates
that beyond structural completeness, the conceptual nature of the user’s
request—specifically distinguishing between isolated objects and complex
environments—must strictly align with the chosen 3D tool’s architectural
boundaries.
